corporate_status_note: MATERIAL: Beazley plc was acquired by Zurich Insurance Group in an all-cash takeover (1,335p/share, comprising 1,310p cash + 25p permitted dividend, ~GBP8.1-8.2bn / ~USD10.8-10.9bn). Shareholders approved the scheme with 99.9% support in April 2026; the scheme became effective on 1 October 2026 when the Court Order was filed with the Registrar of Companies, and Beazley's shares were suspended and delisted from the LSE by 8am on 2 October 2026 (settlement to shareholders due by 15 October 2026). As of this analysis date (10 October 2026), BEZ.L is DELISTED and no longer trades as an independent public company -- it is now a wholly-owned subsidiary of Zurich Insurance Group. This analysis is retained for historical/reference purposes (e.g. understanding the standalone business that Zurich acquired) but the bull/bear case and forward guidance below describe the company as it existed immediately prior to the takeover; there is no longer a tradeable equity security or independent equity story to analyze going forward.
overview: Beazley plc was a London-headquartered specialty insurer and the leading managing agent at Lloyd's of London, underwriting complex, volatile and emerging risks -- most notably as the global market-leading cyber insurer -- across Cyber, Property, Marine/Accident/Political (MAP), and Specialty (D&O, M&A, environmental liability) risk classes. It operated through three distribution platforms (Wholesale/Lloyd's, North America, Europe) and reported in US dollars (~80% of business is USD-denominated) despite its LSE listing and GBP share price. On 1 October 2026 Beazley completed its acquisition by Zurich Insurance Group and was delisted from the London Stock Exchange, becoming a wholly-owned Zurich subsidiary.

business_model.summary: Beazley earns underwriting profit (insurance service result) from premiums on specialty/non-standard risks that traditional insurers avoid, priced using deep technical underwriting expertise, plus investment income earned on the float (premiums held before claims are paid). Revenue (insurance revenue under IFRS 17) was $6.06bn in FY2025 on gross insurance written premiums of $6.10bn; profit is driven by the combined ratio (claims + expenses vs. premium) and the investment return on an ~$12bn investment portfolio. The business is strongly cyclical with the Lloyd's/specialty underwriting cycle -- premium growth and margins expand in 'hard' markets and compress as rates soften, as occurred through 2025-2026.

revenue_streams.name: Property Risks
revenue_streams.trend: growing book, but rates declining sharply (-13.2% in H1 2026)

revenue_streams.name: Cyber Risks (incl. Digital)
revenue_streams.trend: shrinking by design -- Beazley deliberately ceding US market share rather than chase inadequate rates

revenue_streams.name: MAP Risks (Marine, Accident, Political)
revenue_streams.trend: growing, benefiting from geopolitical volatility (Middle East, Marine War)

revenue_streams.name: Net investment income
revenue_streams.trend: growing with larger invested asset base ($12.0bn at FY2025) and currently higher yields

business_model.customer_type: B2B via brokers -- wholesale/Lloyd's brokers, US retail/E&S brokers, and European brokers; ultimate insureds range from large corporates to SMEs (via Digital platform)
business_model.geographic_mix: Platforms: Wholesale/Lloyd's 50% of IWP, North America 42%, Europe 8% (FY2025); business written globally but claims and exposure concentrated in US/UK/Europe
business_model.revenue_nature: Largely annual/renewal-based (not subscription in the SaaS sense, but high retention of renewal business), subject to the underwriting cycle rather than secular recurring growth; short-tail (60%) vs long-tail (40%) claims profile affects reserve duration and investment income

main_competitors: Other Lloyd's managing agents (e.g. Hiscox Syndicate, Brit)
competitive_position.market_position: Global #1 or #2 cyber insurance underwriter by gross written premium (~6.7% global share, narrowly ahead of Chubb at FY2023 data), and one of the largest and most consistently profitable managing agents at Lloyd's of London

moat_factors.description: Two decades of cyber underwriting data, in-house Beazley Security unit, and pioneering the cyber catastrophe ILS/bond market give proprietary risk-selection and pricing insight competitors lack
Syndicate 2623/3622 status at Lloyd's provides access to globally diversified, broker-sourced specialty risk that is difficult for a new entrant to replicate quickly
Repeated Gracechurch broker-service award wins (10 years running) and long broker relationships support submission flow and renewal retention
Three platforms (Wholesale, North America, Europe) and five product divisions let Beazley reallocate capital toward the most rate-adequate lines each year ('lean into and out of' the cycle)
Access to third-party and ILS capital (cyber cat bonds, ILWs) extends underwriting capacity beyond balance-sheet capital

weaknesses: No meaningful switching costs for commercial insurance buyers -- renewal business is price-sensitive and brokers shop the market annually
Underwriting results are inherently volatile and exposed to catastrophe/tail risk (wildfires, hurricanes, cyber catastrophe events)
Concentrated reliance on cyber for brand/profitability even as the company deliberately shrinks that book amid irrational US competition
Smaller balance sheet than diversified multi-line giants (Chubb, AXA, Munich Re), limiting capacity for the largest programmes without reinsurance/ILS support
Now moot given the Zurich acquisition: historical weakness of standalone scale versus global composite insurers was a stated strategic rationale for being acquired

growth_drivers: New Bermuda platform (property treaty, ART/captives, mortgage indemnity, cyber ILS) launched April 2026, targeting $400m of written premium by 2030
Energy transition/renewables underwriting build-out, accelerated by the March 2026 acquisition of kWh Analytics (US renewable energy MGA)
Cyber ILS and catastrophe bond market leadership -- issued the market's first cyber cat bond (2023) and is moving into securitisation/transformation structures via a dedicated ILS fund in 2026
Geographic diversification into Europe and Asia Pacific, which grew faster and at better rate adequacy than the US cyber market in 2025

Secular growth in specialty/complex risk demand: AI-related litigation and cyber exposure, geopolitical risk, data centre and energy infrastructure build-out, nuclear fusion/first-of-kind technology risk

Combination with Zurich (post-close) -- creation of a combined ~$15bn specialty gross written premium platform with expanded distribution, though this growth now accrues to Zurich shareholders, not former Beazley shareholders

business.description: Insurance written premiums fell 1.0% in FY2025 and 4.3% in H1 2026 as rates softened broadly (-6.5% average, -13.2% in Property); Beazley is deliberately ceding volume to protect margin, which compresses near-term growth

Management has explicitly stated it believes much of the US cyber market is pricing below adequacy amid AI-driven and geopolitical risk escalation; Beazley's cyber book shrank 8.8% in 2025 as it refused to chase the market down
Heavy dependence on wholesale/Lloyd's and US E&S broker channels for submission flow
Exposure to secondary perils (convective storms, wildfires, winter freezes), marine war, and cyber catastrophe/systemic AI-driven loss events that can produce outsized single-year losses

financial.description: Reserve confidence level rose to the 91st percentile at H1 2026 (above the preferred 80th-90th range) reflecting heightened uncertainty from softer markets; FY2025 saw a net reserve strengthening of $16.1m (vs. a $144.5m net release in FY2024), driven by Specialty Risks deterioration (social inflation in US health/medical covers)

financial.risk: Investment portfolio interest-rate and credit sensitivity
financial.description: ~$12bn investment portfolio (89% core fixed income, 11% capital growth/equities/hedge funds) is sensitive to rate moves and spread widening; H1 2026 investment return fell to 1.8% from 2.7% in H1 2025 amid market volatility
USD-denominated results (80% of business) reported against a GBP-denominated share price (prior to delisting) and GBP/CAD/EUR cost base (staff salaries) creates translation exposure

regulatory.risk: Lloyd's and Solvency II capital requirements
regulatory.description: Must maintain Solvency II coverage above a 170% minimum target (was 281% at FY2025, ~291% estimated H1 2026) and meet Lloyd's Franchise Board capital/performance standards
EU, UK, Australian and other merger-control approvals were all secured by mid-2026, clearing the way for the 1 October 2026 completion; this risk is now resolved as the deal has closed

macro.description: January 2025 California wildfires and ongoing secondary-peril volatility illustrate rising climate-driven loss costs
Middle East conflict, trade-pattern shifts and marine war risk directly affect MAP Risks claims and demand, cutting both ways (higher losses but also higher demand for specialist cover)

Growth of AI increases both cyber attack sophistication (ransomware, AI-generated attacks) and litigation exposure (AI-related D&O/Specialty claims), a double-edged driver of both demand and loss cost

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global specialty/E&S and cyber insurance markets are in a softening phase of the underwriting cycle after several hard-market years (2020-2023); capacity has returned, pricing power has shifted to buyers, but underlying structural demand (cyber, climate, geopolitical, AI, energy transition risk) continues to grow the addressable specialty risk pool
macro_factors.cyclicality: High -- both from the insurance underwriting cycle (pricing/capacity) and catastrophe loss experience (weather, cyber events)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high via the ~$12bn investment book (duration ~1.6-1.7 years) and the IFRS 17 discounting of insurance liabilities, which produces a sizeable net insurance finance expense/income line sensitive to yield curve moves
key_input_costs: Claims inflation (social inflation in US casualty/Specialty lines)

recent_developments.event: Beazley and Zurich Insurance Group announced a recommended all-cash offer by Zurich for the entire share capital of Beazley at 1,335p/share (1,310p cash + 25p dividend), valuing Beazley at ~GBP8.1-8.2bn
Beazley announced acquisition of kWh Analytics, a US renewable energy MGA, to strengthen its Transition underwriting capabilities
Beazley shareholders approved the Zurich scheme of arrangement with ~99.9% of votes cast in favour
Beazley began underwriting property treaty business from its new Bermuda platform, exceeding initial targets ahead of the 1 April reinsurance renewal
European Commission granted EU merger-control approval for the Zurich/Beazley transaction; Australian competition clearance also secured around this period

H1 2026 results: insurance written premiums down 4.3% YoY as rates fell an average 6.5% (Property Risks down 13.2%); profit before tax fell to $237.7m (H1 2025: $502.5m) including $33.6m of Zurich transaction costs; discounted combined ratio deteriorated to 88.4% (H1 2025: 80.3%); annualised ROE fell to 7.6% (H1 2025: 18.2%)
Zurich's acquisition of Beazley became effective (Court Order filed with the Registrar of Companies); deal valued at ~GBP8.1bn (~USD10.8-10.9bn)
Beazley shares suspended and delisted from the London Stock Exchange; shareholder cash settlement due by 15 October 2026

guidance.as_of: H1 2026 Interim Report / FY2025 Annual Report (last guidance issued as an independent company)
guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (final year as a standalone public company; guidance is now moot following the 1 October 2026 acquisition close)

items.target: mid single-digit growth across the cycle
items.notes: FY2025 and H1 2026 both show premium contraction (-1.0% and -4.3% respectively) as management deliberately prioritises rate adequacy over volume in a softening market
FY2025 undiscounted COR was 81.2% (2024: 79.0%); H1 2026 undiscounted COR deteriorated to 93.3% (H1 2025: 84.9%), still within but near the top of the targeted range

10-year average ROE of 15.5% and 5-year average of 22.2% through FY2025; H1 2026 annualised ROE fell sharply to 7.6% (9.1% adjusted for Zurich deal costs and a normalised capital distribution), reflecting the current soft market and one-off transaction costs
Property treaty underwriting from Bermuda commenced 1 April 2026 and exceeded initial targets in its first months

items.target: Solvency II coverage ratio maintained above 170% of SCR minimum, with surplus above growth/volatility buffers returned to shareholders
items.notes: Solvency II ratio was 281% at FY2025 and estimated 291% at H1 2026, both well above the stated minimum

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Adrian Cox emphasised that softening rates (particularly in Property and US cyber) require continued underwriting discipline rather than chasing volume, while highlighting Bermuda, transition underwriting (kWh Analytics acquisition) and cyber ILS as the key idiosyncratic growth levers for 2026 and beyond. All forward guidance is now superseded by the completed Zurich acquisition; Beazley will no longer report independent financial guidance as a standalone listed entity.

bull_case: NOTE: Moot for new investment decisions -- BEZ.L completed its acquisition by Zurich Insurance Group on 1 October 2026 and was delisted from the LSE on 2 October 2026; there is no longer an independently tradeable equity

Historically: global leadership in cyber insurance underwriting with two decades of proprietary claims/risk data and the market's first cyber catastrophe bond, a durable structural moat as cyber risk grows with AI adoption
Historically: consistent long-term track record of value creation -- 10-year average ROE of 15.5%, 5-year average of 22.2%, and over $2.5bn returned to shareholders since 2011

Historically: diversified platform (three distribution channels, five product divisions) gave genuine flexibility to lean into the most rate-adequate lines each cycle rather than being a one-trick cyber underwriter

The Zurich transaction itself delivered shareholders a certain, immediate cash return at a ~60% premium to the undisturbed share price, crystallising value rather than leaving it exposed to a softening underwriting cycle

New growth optionality (Bermuda, transition/renewables, cyber ILS) now benefits from Zurich's larger balance sheet and distribution reach rather than being capital-constrained as a standalone Lloyd's specialist
bear_case: There is no bear case for new investment -- the stock is delisted and cash-settled; any residual bear thesis only applies retrospectively to the standalone business or prospectively to Zurich (ZURN) as the acquirer

Historically: premium and combined ratio were deteriorating sharply into the deal close -- H1 2026 insurance written premiums down 4.3%, undiscounted COR up to 93.3% from 84.9%, and ROE collapsing to 7.6% from 18.2%, evidence of a hard pricing cycle unwinding quickly
Historically: deliberate retreat from the US cyber market (down 8.8% in 2025) ceded share in Beazley's flagship franchise to competitors willing to underwrite at thinner margins

Historically: reserve confidence crept above the preferred 80th-90th percentile range (91st percentile at H1 2026), and FY2025 saw a net reserve strengthening (vs. releases in prior years) driven by social inflation in US Specialty/health lines -- an early warning sign on reserve adequacy

Historically: heavy exposure to catastrophe tail risk (wildfires, marine war, cyber catastrophe) made annual results volatile and dependent on a benign loss environment, as seen in the swing from FY2024's $1.42bn PBT to FY2025's $1.15bn PBT amid the January 2025 California wildfires
